entities.summary:
Originating on the Indian subcontinent around 5000 BCE, Indian religions represent a diverse family of spiritual traditions that have profoundly shaped global civilization. Encompassing Hinduism, Buddhism, Jainism, Sikhism, and various indigenous belief systems, these traditions are not merely sets of doctrines but comprehensive ways of life, providing philosophical frameworks, ethical guidelines, and cultural practices for billions. Their historical significance lies in their deep antiquity, their continuous evolution over millennia, and their pervasive influence on art, literature, governance, and social structures across Asia and beyond, making them foundational pillars of human thought.

The development of Indian religions can be traced from the early Bronze Age Indus Valley Civilization, through the Vedic period (c. 1500–500 BCE) with its foundational hymns and rituals, to the philosophical ferment of the Upanishadic era (c. 800–200 BCE). This period witnessed the emergence of core concepts like karma, dharma, moksha, and samsara, and the rise of ascetic Sramana traditions, notably Buddhism, founded by Siddhartha Gautama (c. 563–483 BCE), and Jainism, revitalized by Mahavira (c. 599–527 BCE). Subsequent centuries saw the flourishing of diverse Hindu schools (Vedanta, Yoga, Nyaya, Vaisheshika, Mimamsa, Samkhya), the devotional Bhakti movements, and the syncretic emergence of Sikhism in the 15th century CE under Guru Nanak Dev Ji, each contributing unique perspectives on deity, self, and liberation.
